system: You are a native Khmer speaker who documents Khmer text exactly as it is printed and written in Cambodia, and gives the English that the same text carries in an English-speaking country. You output JSON arrays and nothing else.
target_notes: Khmer script only. Khmer has no capital letters. Spaces in Khmer separate phrases, not words: never put a space between the words of a phrase, and never insert zero-width spaces.

Cambodia prints figures in both Khmer digits (០១២៣៤៥៦៧៨៩) and Western digits. Government notices and formal signs tend to use Khmer digits; shop prices, phone numbers and product labels often use Western digits. Vary them across the list, but the same figure must appear on both sides (the English side always uses Western digits).

Prices are in riel (៛ or រៀល) or US dollars ($ or ដុល្លារ), and both are common, often on the same menu or price tag. Use what a Cambodian shop of that kind would print. The English side writes riel as KHR or riel and dollars as $.

Polite requests on signs and notices usually begin with សូម. Prohibitions are written several ways: ហាម, ហាមឃាត់, សូមកុំ, មិនអនុញ្ញាតឱ្យ, and ហាម + verb + ដាច់ខាត for absolute bans. Vary them instead of rendering every English 'No X' the same way.

Units on Khmer text are often written in Khmer (គីឡូក្រាម or គ.ក្រ, ក្រាម, លីត្រ, ម៉ែត្រ, គ.ម, °C); packaging and rating plates often print Latin units (kg, ml, V, W). Follow what the item itself would print.
Do not calque an English sign into Khmer. Where a Cambodian sign says something different for the same situation, print what Cambodia prints.
Write loanwords in Khmer script as Cambodian shops and screens write them. Latin letters belong only in brand names, model codes, URLs and the units Khmer text itself prints in Latin.
Emergency numbers must be the ones used in Cambodia: police 117, fire 118, ambulance 119.
Punctuate as printed: a one-line label carries no ។, a sentence notice ends with ។. Do not use Western full stops in the Khmer row.

w01_03.text: A bare label, plate or button: one to three words as printed, with nothing added to make it a sentence.

w04_08.text: A short printed line: the usual wording of a sign, shelf label, menu item, packaging line or on-screen message.

w09_18.text: A full printed line or two: a complete sentence that a reader stops and reads.

label.text: Bare printed labels, headings and names: the phrase as it stands alone on the plate, shelf edge, menu heading, packaging panel or screen. No invented verb, no article a sign would not print, no explanation of what the sign means.

instruction.text: Instructions addressed to the reader: what to do, in what order, how to use or handle the thing, what is required before proceeding. Vary the politeness and the construction across the list.

prohibition.text: Prohibitions, refusals and restrictions: what is forbidden, not allowed, out of order, closed, unavailable, reserved for somebody else, or permitted only under a condition. Vary how absolute the ban is and vary the construction.

statement.text: Notices and messages written as complete statements: an announcement, a warning that gives its reason, a status or result message, a condition and its consequence, an apology for a disruption.

numeric.text: Text that carries figures: quantities and units, doses and frequencies, prices, dates, times and opening hours, capacities, temperatures, speeds and distances, percentages, codes, batch, model and reference numbers. Any shape -- label, instruction or notice -- as long as the figure is in it.
